                                       PROJECT NO. 58482

 Large Load Demand Management Service                §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
                                                     §
                                                     §                 OF TEXAS
                                                     §
                                                     §


April 8, 2026




                                     CYRUSONE COMMENTS

       CyrusOne, LP (“CyrusOne” or the “Company”) is a leading global data center developer
and operator, providing mission-critical infrastructure for cloud providers, enterprises, and
hyperscale customers. Headquartered in Texas, CyrusOne operates more than 60 data centers
worldwide, including a significant presence in Texas. Our operations rely on dependable, robust,
and economical electricity to support high-density computing environments that enable digital
transformation across industries. Our facilities serve over 1,000 customers, including
approximately 200 Fortune 1000 companies, CyrusOne’s leading global platform of hybrid-cloud
and multi-cloud deployments offers customers colocation, hyperscale and build-to-suit
environments, which help enhance the strategic connections of their essential data
infrastructures and support the achievement of sustainability goals. CyrusOne data centers offer
world-class flexibility, enabling clients to modernize, simplify and rapidly respond to changing
demands. Combining exceptional financial strength, a broad global footprint and continued
investment in key digital gateway markets, CyrusOne provides the world’s largest companies
with long-term stability and strategic advantages at scale.

       CyrusOne welcomes the opportunity to provide comments to the Public Utility
Commission of Texas (“Commission”) and the Commission’s Staff (“Staff”) in Project No. 58482,
Large Load Demand Management Service (“Service”). We welcome the opportunity to work
with the Commission, Staff, and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (“ERCOT”) on framing
this Service.

                                                 1
                                           INTRODUCTION

       CyrusOne recognizes the Commissions critical role in shaping the implementation of
Texas Senate Bill 6 (“SB 6”) in a way that aligns with existing regulatory and legal frameworks in
place, while addressing key policy decisions to enable large load customers to site and
interconnect into the electric grid. CyrusOne is actively developing, building, and operating data
centers across the state of Texas and the Commissions implementation of this Service is
important in how we think about the design, construction, operations, and maintenance of our
data centers and any onsite energy infrastructure.

   1. Of the two options described in the attached slides, an as-needed service or a seasonal
      service, which is the better option to implement PURA § 39.170(b) and why?

       It is our understanding that this Service is intended to provide a reliable, pre‑identified
resource capable of delivering material reliability benefits to the electric grid in advance of
anticipated extreme weather events. Consistent with prior Commission direction and ERCOT
reliability programs, resources participating in this Service would be compensated in exchange
for making capacity available to support system reliability when conditions warrant.

       Given the anticipatory nature of the Service, we recommend that Commission Staff, the
Commission, and ERCOT establish clear, standardized protocols that allow resources to register
and qualify in advance of an anticipated event. A pre‑registration framework would help ensure
that participating resources have demonstrated their ability to perform when called and would
provide ERCOT with greater confidence regarding the magnitude and availability of committed
capacity.

       While ERCOT may often have advance notice of severe weather, there will inevitably be
circumstances in which changing forecasts or localized weather conditions create rapidly
escalating reliability concerns. In those instances, the Commission should avoid an approach that
relies on last‑minute identification of eligible resources or ad hoc determinations of potential
curtailment capability. Such an approach increases operational uncertainty and undermines the
reliability value the Service is intended to provide.


                                                  2
        A standardized and pre‑planned structure would align with existing ERCOT protocols
governing other reliability services, including the use of advance qualification, defined
operational parameters, and clear performance obligations. This approach would also provide
large load customers operating complex facilities with the predictability needed to incorporate
participation into their operational planning. A repeatable and well‑defined process allows
participants to execute curtailment obligations consistently and effectively as extreme weather
events unfold, rather than reacting in real time under uncertain conditions.

       Accordingly, we recommend that the Commission direct ERCOT to implement this Service
through an advance qualification and registration framework, consistent with existing ERCOT
reliability service constructs, under which participating resources are identified, validated, and
enrolled ahead of anticipated extreme weather events. This framework should include clearly
defined operational requirements, notification timelines, and performance expectations. Doing
so will ensure that the Service delivers predictable and dependable reliability value, remains
administratively manageable for ERCOT, and provides participating resources with the certainty
necessary to commit capacity in a manner fully aligned with prior PUCT orders and ERCOT
protocols.

   2. PURA § 39.170(b) states the commission must require ERCOT to develop a reliability
      service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency condition. PURA § 39.
      l 70(b)(I) states the rules governing the new service must specify the periods when the
      service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme weather
      events.
      a. Does PURA authorize ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances other than
          extreme weather events? If yes, what kind of events?
      b. Should the commission define "extreme weather event'' and, if so, how should it be
          defined?

       The Texas Legislature advanced multiple related objectives through the enactment of SB
6, including supporting continued economic development while strengthening tools available to
manage grid reliability as large electric loads continue to locate in the state. As Texas attracts a
growing number of large load customers, reliability programs such as this Service can play an



                                                 3
 important role in helping ERCOT and the Commission manage system conditions both in
anticipation of and during extreme weather events impacting the electric grid.

       As Staff has appropriately noted, the Legislature did not define the term “extreme weather
events” within SB 6 or PURA §39.170. Rather than viewing this omission as a limitation, we believe
it provides a deliberate opportunity for Staff, the Commission, and ERCOT to design the Service
in a manner that is consistent with how the electric grid is actually planned and operated in
response to weather‑driven reliability risks. Establishing a rigid or overly prescriptive definition of
“extreme weather events” may be difficult given regional variation across the ERCOT footprint
and evolving forecast conditions. Instead, the Service should be structured to align with ERCOT’s
existing hierarchy of reliability actions, including the steps taken in advance of, and leading up to,
Energy Emergency Alert (“EEA”) events.

       Under current ERCOT protocols, EEA declarations and associated curtailment actions are
triggered by system‑wide reliability conditions, with load shed executed locally by TDSPs on a
feeder‑by‑feeder basis. This framework underscores the value of reliability tools that can be
deployed prior to emergency conditions, particularly those that address localized or emerging
risks before they require system‑wide emergency actions. A properly designed Service, consistent
with PURA §39.170(b), could complement ERCOT’s EEA process by providing a structured,
pre‑identified resource that enhances operational flexibility and may, in some circumstances,
mitigate the need for ERCOT to escalate to emergency declarations.

       Consistent with SB 6, the Legislature also sought to encourage large load customers to
pursue net‑metered arrangements with existing and new behind‑the‑meter and colocated
generation. Large loads participating under such arrangements can provide meaningful reliability
value when supported by clear, predictable protocols governing when and how curtailment may
be deployed in response to weather‑related system conditions. Large loads should not be
explicitly excluded from participating in this Service if they enter into a net metering arrangement
as there are several design configurations in which a large load customer could be called under
this Service to curtail and then be curtailed (which could include curtailing load from a colocated
generator and onsite batteries and power plant equipment) effectively allowing for the generator

                                                  4
 to meet SB 6 requirements for net metered loads and allowing the large load customer to inject
additional capacity under this Service into the electric grid. Given the size of the ERCOT system,
the scale of new large loads, and the importance of maintaining reliability for all Texas customers,
we believe that Staff, the Commission, and ERCOT should provide greater clarity regarding the
guidelines, definitions, and deployment protocols associated with this Service. Doing so will
ensure that the Service functions as an effective reliability tool that is aligned with both legislative
intent and ERCOT’s established operational practices.

        We encourage Staff, the Commission, and ERCOT contemplate how to leverage this Service
in various scenarios that may lead to a broader need to issue an Energy Emergency Alert (“EEA”)
because of anticipated concerns tied to extreme weather. Examples to consider include, but are
not limited to:

    1. Load pockets with limited import capability.
        Certain areas of the ERCOT system have constrained transmission import capability and
        may become vulnerable during extreme weather events even when system‑wide
        reserves remain sufficient. In these locations, elevated demand combined with
        weather‑related stress can quickly erode available capacity, creating localized reliability
        concerns that could be addressed through targeted deployment of the Service before
        broader emergency actions are required.
    2. Deferred or delayed transmission or substation infrastructure.
        Delays in planned infrastructure upgrades, including substation expansions, transformer
        replacements, or other transmission improvements, can increase exposure to extreme
        weather impacts. When such delays coincide with seasonal peak load and adverse
        weather conditions, localized capacity constraints may emerge that would benefit from
        advance, targeted curtailment through the Service.
    3. Outage of a single high‑voltage transmission element.
        The loss of a major transmission facility, such as a 345‑kV line, can materially reduce
        transfer capability into a region. While the ERCOT system as a whole may remain
        reliable, the outage of a single critical element, when coupled with extreme or localized


                                                   5
        weather, can create acute localized reliability risks that may warrant preemptive action
       to avoid escalation into system‑wide EEA conditions.
   4. Cascading impacts from localized extreme weather events.
        Extreme weather affecting a specific geographic area, including prolonged heat,
       localized freezing conditions, or severe storms, can simultaneously increase load and
       reduce generation availability within that area. These cascading effects may not
       immediately trigger a system‑wide emergency but can rapidly deteriorate local
       reliability. Leveraging the Service in advance of these circumstances could help stabilize
       affected areas and reduce the likelihood that localized disruptions propagate into
       broader EEA declarations.


   3. PURA § 39.170(b)(3) states the rules governing the new service must prohibit
      participation by any large load customer that curtails in response to the wholesale price
      of electricity, as determined by ERCOT, or that otherwise participates in a different
      reliability or ancillary service. PURA§ 37.056 l(e)-which allows ERCOT to direct a large
      load customer with onsite backup generation to either curtail its load or deploy its
      backup generation under certain circumstances-states that a large load customer with
      onsite backup generation may participate in a service authorized by PURA§ 39.170(b).
      a. What type of qualification is necessary to show that it may take a large load
          customer 24 hours to ramp down safely?

       As noted above, we recommend that Commission Staff, the Commission, and ERCOT
develop clear guidelines, definitions, and deployment protocols to establish a shared and
common understanding of the intent, structure, and operation of the Service. These protocols
should clearly address how the Service will be managed, what expectations apply to participating
large load customers, how compensation will be determined, and what requirements must be
satisfied to qualify as an eligible resource. Providing this clarity is essential to ensuring that
participating resources can make informed commitments and that the Service delivers reliable
and predictable value to grid operations.

       In developing these protocols, additional clarification is needed regarding the distinction
between an “as‑needed” and a “seasonal” Service. Under our understanding, an “as‑needed”
construct would imply that the Service exists, but eligible large load participants are identified
                                                6
 and enrolled only immediately prior to an anticipated extreme weather or emergency condition.
By contrast, a “seasonal” construct would involve identifying, qualifying, and enrolling
participating resources in advance, with large loads having clear notice that they may be called
upon during a defined time period.

        We believe that a “seasonal” approach is more workable and better aligned with the
operational realities of large load facilities, including data centers. Advance enrollment allows
operators to conduct periodic testing, confirm willingness to participate, and validate operational
capabilities prior to an event. It also enables participants to clearly define ramp rates, test internal
systems, and ensure that onsite equipment and procedures can perform as required when the
Service is activated. This advance preparation is particularly important where partial curtailment,
rather than full shutdown, is expected.

        Depending on system needs, a large load exceeding 75 MW may be asked to curtail all or
only a portion of its load. For example, a 400 MW data center may be requested to curtail 100
MW within a 24‑hour time frame. The actual time needed to achieve that reduction can vary
significantly depending on the facility’s electrical configuration, applicable Service Level
Agreements, and installed onsite equipment. In some cases, load reductions can be implemented
within minutes; in others, shifting or curtailing a portion of load may require additional
coordination, sequencing, and operational adjustments to maintain reliability within the facility.

        For this reason, we encourage that the guidelines and deployment protocols clearly
identify which resources will be called during curtailment events, the expected magnitude of
curtailment, and the applicable notification and performance timelines. While full curtailment of
an entire facility may be achieved quickly in certain configurations, partial curtailment scenarios
often require more deliberate operational steps and cannot be executed instantaneously without
prior planning. Establishing clear, advance expectations will allow participating large load
customers to respond efficiently and reliably, while ensuring that ERCOT receives dependable and
timely reliability support when system conditions warrant.

        b. What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39. l 70(b), if any, should apply
           to participation in the new service?
                                                   7
        PURA §39.170 establishes a targeted reliability service intended to support ERCOT’s ability
to manage grid conditions during extreme weather events, while setting forth specific and limited
eligibility restrictions. The statute expressly prohibits participation only where a large load
customer curtails in response to wholesale electricity prices determined by ERCOT or otherwise
participates in a different reliability or ancillary service. Beyond these enumerated limitations, the
Legislature did not impose additional prohibitions on eligibility. Notably, the statute does not
restrict participation by large load customers that operate under Commission‑approved
net‑metering arrangements, nor does it exclude loads colocated with generation. Under
well‑established principles of statutory interpretation, eligibility exclusions should be confined to
those expressly identified by the Legislature and should not be expanded through implication or
administrative interpretation.

       A Commission‑approved net‑metering arrangement does not, by itself, constitute
participation in an ERCOT market product, reliability service, or ancillary service. Net metering
governs the measurement and settlement of energy flows between a load and colocated
generation; it does not establish performance obligations, price exposure, or compensation
mechanisms comparable to ERCOT reliability or ancillary services. Treating net‑metered entities
as ineligible would improperly conflate metering and settlement structures with market
participation. A large load with onsite or colocated generation remains an end‑use customer
capable of providing load curtailment and operational flexibility. Eligibility for the Service should
therefore be assessed based on operational behavior and performance capability, rather than the
presence of a net‑metering configuration.

       Allowing participation by colocated large loads can meaningfully enhance grid reliability
and is fully consistent with the objectives of PURA §39.170. In many cases, a large load co-located
next to a generation resource may receive all or a portion of its normal operating power from that
facility. During grid emergencies, the generator may reduce service to the colocated load and
export power to the ERCOT grid, increasing system supply. At the same time, the large load may
curtail part or all of its demand, operate onsite emergency generation, or dispatch battery energy
storage resources to further reduce net load. These actions provide reliability benefits that are


                                                  8
 equivalent to, and in some cases exceed, traditional curtailment mechanisms, particularly when
they can be executed pursuant to pre‑planned operational protocols. Excluding such
arrangements would unnecessarily eliminate resources that are capable of delivering reliable,
measurable, and controllable support during periods of system stress.

        Exclusion of net‑metered, colocated large loads would also conflict with the Legislature’s
intent in enacting SB 6. SB 6 explicitly encouraged large load customers to pursue net‑metered
and colocated arrangements with generation as a means to accelerate economic development,
reduce pressure on the transmission system, and improve overall grid reliability. Interpreting
PURA §39.170 to prohibit participation by those same arrangements would undermine that policy
objective and create a disincentive for investments the Legislature sought to promote. Nothing in
the statutory framework suggests an intent to penalize large load customers that have invested
in facilities designed to align with reliability goals.

        Accordingly, CyrusOne respectfully submits that no additional prohibitions beyond those
expressly stated in PURA §39.170(b) should apply to participation in the Service. Net‑metered
large load customers approved under SB 6 should remain eligible, provided they do not engage
in price‑responsive curtailment or participate in overlapping ERCOT reliability or ancillary
services. Eligibility determinations should focus on operational conduct and performance, not
metering structure. Allowing participation by net‑metered, colocated large loads will broaden the
pool of reliable resources available to ERCOT, enhance system resilience, and further the
Legislature’s dual objectives of maintaining grid reliability and supporting continued economic
development in Texas..

        c. Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such as four
           coincident peak (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude participation in the new
           service?
        From the standpoint of a data center operator, participation in price responsiveness aimed
at managing transmission-related cost exposure—such as the Four Coincident Peak (“4CP”)
methodology or any successor approach—should not, standing alone, disqualify a load from
participating in the new Service. These activities address different problems and operate on
different time horizons. Price responsiveness to transmission cost drivers is a routine,
                                                    9
 economically rational practice that helps customers manage long‑term cost allocation and
informs planning outcomes. By contrast, the Service contemplated under PURA § 39.170(b) is a
narrowly tailored reliability tool, intended for infrequent deployment during extreme weather
driven by emergency conditions and likely subject to specific notice, duration, and performance
requirements.
       A blanket prohibition based on 4CP participation would likely exclude exactly the types of
large, operationally sophisticated loads that are best positioned to provide dependable,
measurable curtailment at the scale envisioned by the statute. Such an outcome would weaken
the effectiveness of the service without advancing reliability objectives. The more appropriate
regulatory concern is not whether a participant engages in price-responsive behavior in other
contexts, but whether the same load reduction is being counted or compensated twice. That issue
can be addressed through clear eligibility criteria, disclosure requirements, and post‑event
verification to ensure that curtailments provided under the new service are incremental,
reliability‑driven, and distinct from routine cost-management actions, while still allowing large
loads to engage responsibly in both frameworks.


       d. Should the commission define ''curtailment in response to wholesale price of
          electricity'' and, if so, how should it be defined?

We do not have a current position on how it should be defined, but reserve the right to provide
perspective at a later date.

   4. How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new service?

       This Service should be structured and deployed as a credible, last‑resort reliability
backstop intended for use during extreme weather conditions, rather than as a standing capacity
product or an economic demand response mechanism. Its purpose should be narrowly tailored
to support ERCOT’s ability to manage acute system reliability risks, and it should function as a
complement to—rather than a replacement for—existing tools such as emergency reserves,
emergency imports, and ERCOT’s established EEA framework. Preserving this distinction is
essential to maintaining the Service’s emergency character and ensuring it is leveraged only when
system conditions warrant.

                                               10
        To that end, a reasonable target quantity for the Service would be on the order of 1–5
percent of ERCOT’s forecasted peak load for applicable extreme weather seasons, with the target
recalculated annually to reflect changing system conditions and load growth. Establishing a
defined MW target provides predictability for participating resources and gives ERCOT confidence
that a known quantity of committed and callable capacity will be available during critical periods,
without creating incentives for over‑procurement or routine use.

       From a budget and pricing perspective, we encourage the Commission and ERCOT to
adopt a clearly defined annual or seasonal budget cap for the Service that is pre‑approved,
transparent, and subject to periodic review with stakeholder input. Budget sizing should be
informed by the targeted MW quantity and the maximum anticipated duration of deployment
under emergency conditions. A defined budget framework protects against excessive
procurement, provides participating large loads with clarity that compensation reflects the true
emergency value of the Service, and supports ERCOT’s operational planning objectives. Given the
Service’s intended role as an infrequently deployed reliability backstop, pricing should
appropriately reflect its limited and emergency‑driven use, rather than incentivizing routine
dispatch or participation for economic reasons.

   5. What additional information should the Commission consider in its implementation of
      PURA§ 39.170(b)?

       In implementing PURA §39.170(b), it would be beneficial for the Commission to provide
clarity regarding how the Service is intended to function in circumstances involving localized or
targeted reliability constraints, rather than solely system‑wide emergency conditions. While
ERCOT’s Energy Emergency Alert (EEA) framework appropriately addresses broader system
reliability issues, experience has shown that extreme weather events often interact with localized
infrastructure limitations in ways that can create acute reliability risks absent a system‑wide
emergency declaration. Examples include load pockets with limited import capability, delayed or
deferred substation or transformer upgrades, or the outage of a single large transmission
element, such as a 345‑kV line. Under normal conditions, these constraints may be manageable;



                                                11
 however, when compounded by localized extreme weather, they may result in localized
emergency conditions that warrant targeted reliability interventions.

       As the Commission considers how the Service may be deployed to address these localized
risks, it is also important to consider the practical characteristics of the resources that would be
expected to respond, particularly large loads with backup generation assets. Many large load
facilities, including data centers, maintain onsite diesel generation fleets designed first and
foremost for reliability and safety, not continuous operation. These fleets may include a
combination of Tier 2 and Tier 4 engines, each governed by different air emissions standards and
operating limitations. Participation in the Service may require these resources to operate outside
traditional assumptions for backup generator usage, particularly if activation occurs in
anticipation of extreme weather rather than during a clearly defined emergency.

       From an air permitting perspective, it is not yet clear whether operation under this Service
would qualify as “emergency” operation for purposes of federal or state air emissions
requirements. If Service deployment occurs preemptively—prior to an EEA declaration or prior to
conditions meeting traditional emergency definitions—runtime associated with participation
may not clearly fall within existing emergency exemptions under Clean Air Act permitting
frameworks. This distinction has material implications for large load participants, as generators
may require updated permits or permit modifications to lawfully support participation in the
Service.

       Accordingly, we believe it is critical for the Commission to coordinate closely with the
Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (“TCEQ”) and, where appropriate, the U.S.
Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”), to ensure that expectations for generator operation
under the Service are clearly understood and consistently applied. Participants need clarity
regarding the range of potential operating scenarios that may be expected under the Service,
including anticipated duration, frequency, and notice periods for generator operation. Such clarity
is essential to determine whether additional permitting is required and to avoid creating
regulatory uncertainty that could discourage participation.


                                                12
        As part of this coordination, it would be helpful for the Commission and TCEQ to consider
whether enforcement discretion or other compliance assurances may be appropriate in narrowly
defined circumstances where generator operation is undertaken in good‑faith compliance with
the Service to support grid reliability, particularly where deviations from permit conditions are
limited in duration and not indicative of routine or prolonged non‑compliance. While we
recognize that air quality protections remain paramount, clear guidance on how agencies intend
to treat generator operation undertaken at ERCOT’s direction or in coordination with
Commission‑approved reliability programs would meaningfully reduce uncertainty for
participants.

       Ultimately, thoughtful alignment between the PUCT, ERCOT, TCEQ, and EPA will be
essential to the successful implementation of PURA §39.170(b). Providing clarity on
environmental compliance expectations will enable large loads with backup generation to assess
participation realistically, ensure adherence to applicable emissions requirements, and support
the Service’s reliability objectives without unintended regulatory conflicts.

   6. PURA §39. l 70(a) states: The commission shall require the independent organization
      certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region to ensure that each electric
      cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, and municipally owned utility serving
      a transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol, including the installation of any
      necessary equipment or technology before the customer is interconnected, to allow the
      load to be curtailed during firm load shed. The electric cooperative transmission and
      distribution utility, or municipally owned utility shall confer with the +customer to the
      extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated manner. This subsection applies only to a
      load interconnected after December 31, 2025, that is not: (1) Load operated by a critical
      load industrial customer, as defined by Section 17.002; or (2)Designated as a critical
      natural gas facility under Section 38.074. Should the Commission include in this
      rulemaking a directive implementing PURA §39. l70{a)?

       The Commission should address the requirements of PURA §39.170(a) in this rulemaking
to the extent necessary to ensure clarity, consistency, and coordinated implementation,
particularly given the operational overlap between firm load shed obligations and the Service
contemplated under PURA §39.170(b). Section 39.170(a) directs ERCOT to ensure that


                                                13
 transmission and distribution service providers and municipally owned utilities serving new
transmission‑voltage customers develop curtailment protocols and associated equipment to
enable firm load shed, in coordination with customers, for loads interconnected after December
31, 2025. While this obligation is distinct from the reliability Service under consideration, the
two provisions operate within the same hierarchy of load management during emergency
conditions. Including a directive or clarification within this rulemaking would help avoid
conflicting expectations, ensure that firm load shed capabilities developed under subsection (a)
are appropriately aligned with participation frameworks under subsection (b), and reinforce the
importance of coordinated curtailment that reflects both grid reliability needs and customer
operational realities. At the same time, any Commission action should avoid duplicative
requirements or prescriptive implementation details that may already be addressed through
ERCOT protocols or separate interconnection and distribution planning processes. Clarifying
how these statutory provisions are intended to coexist would provide needed regulatory
certainty for utilities, ERCOT, and large load customers alike.

                                           CONCLUSION

       CyrusOne appreciates consideration of these comments and recommendations. We look
forward to working collaboratively with Commission Staff and the Commission and encourage
continued dialogue on this topic as the Commission, Staff, ERCOT, and stakeholders.



                                                   Respectfully submitted,
                                                   By: Kevin Marquardt
                                                   Kevin Marquardt
                                                   CyrusOne
                                                   Director, Energy Policy & Regulatory Affairs

                                                 14
                                      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Each set of comments should include a standalone executive summary as the last page of the
filing. This executive summary must be clearly labeled with the submitting entity's name and list
each substantive recommendation made in the comments.

RECOMMENDATIONS MADE BY CYRUSONE

   1. Implement the Service as an Advance‑Qualified Reliability Resource
       The Commission should direct ERCOT to implement the Service through an advance
       qualification and registration framework that identifies, validates, and enrolls
       participating resources prior to anticipated extreme weather events, rather than relying
       on ad hoc or real‑time procurement.
   2. Adopt a Pre‑Planned, Standardized Participation Structure
        The Commission, Staff, and ERCOT should establish clear, standardized guidelines,
       definitions, and deployment protocols that define how the Service will be managed,
       what operational expectations apply to participating large loads, how compensation will
       be determined, and what requirements must be satisfied to demonstrate eligibility.
   3. Favor a “Seasonal” Service Design Over an “As‑Needed” Model
        The Commission should adopt a seasonal structure for the Service, under which
       participating large loads are identified and enrolled in advance for defined periods,
       rather than an “as‑needed” approach that relies on last‑minute identification
       immediately prior to an emergency.
   4. Require Advance Testing and Ramp‑Rate Verification
        The Service design should allow participating large loads to conduct periodic testing,
       validate ramp rates, and confirm operational readiness prior to deployment, recognizing
       that partial curtailment may require more time and coordination than full shutdown.
   5. Avoid Last‑Minute Identification of Curtailable Resources
        The Commission should avoid a Service construct that requires ERCOT to scramble
       during emerging emergencies to identify which resources can curtail and by how much,
       as this undermines operational certainty and the reliability value of the Service.



                                                15
 6. Align Service Deployment With ERCOT’s EEA Hierarchy
    The Service should be designed to complement, not replace, ERCOT’s existing Energy
   Emergency Alert (EEA) framework and other emergency tools, and should be deployable
   in advance of system‑wide EEA declarations.
7. Permit Use of the Service for Localized or Targeted Reliability Events
    The Commission should clarify that the Service may be used to address localized or
   cascading reliability risks tied to extreme weather, including load pockets with limited
   import capability, deferred infrastructure, transmission outages, or localized weather
   impacts, even where system‑wide reserves remain adequate.
8. Do Not Impose Additional Eligibility Prohibitions Beyond PURA §39.170(b)
    Eligibility for the Service should be limited to only those prohibitions expressly stated in
   statute, and the Commission should not expand eligibility exclusions through implication
   or administrative interpretation.
9. Allow Participation by Net‑Metered and Colocated Large Loads
    Large loads operating under Commission‑approved net‑metering arrangements or
   colocated with generation should not be excluded from participation, provided they do
   not engage in price‑responsive curtailment or participate in overlapping ERCOT reliability
   or ancillary services.
10. Evaluate Eligibility Based on Operational Behavior, Not Metering Structure
    The Commission and ERCOT should assess eligibility for participation based on actual
   operational conduct and performance capability, rather than the presence of a
   net‑metering or colocated generation configuration.
11. Permit Participation by Loads Engaged in Transmission Cost Management (e.g., 4CP)
    Participation in transmission cost‑management practices such as Four Coincident Peak
   (4CP) or successor methodologies should not, by itself, disqualify a large load from
   participating in the Service, provided curtailments are not double‑counted or
   compensated.
12. Establish Clear Qualification Criteria for Load Ramp‑Down Timeframes
    The Commission and ERCOT should define qualification standards that recognize some


                                             16
    large loads may require up to 24 hours to safely achieve full or partial curtailment,
   depending on configuration, SLAs, and onsite equipment.
13. Define Clear Notification, Performance, and Magnitude Expectations
    Deployment protocols should clearly identify which resources will be called, the amount
   of curtailment expected, and applicable notification and performance timelines to
   enable reliable and orderly execution.
14. Structure the Service as a Last‑Resort Reliability Backstop
    The Service should be explicitly designed as an infrequently used, last‑resort reliability
   tool for extreme weather conditions, not as a standing capacity product or economic
   demand response mechanism.
15. Set a Reasonable MW Target Based on Seasonal Peak Load
    The Commission should establish a target quantity for the Service of approximately 1–5
   percent of ERCOT’s forecasted peak load during extreme weather seasons and
   recalculate the target annually.
16. Adopt a Transparent, Pre‑Approved Budget Cap
    The Commission and ERCOT should establish a clearly defined annual or seasonal
   budget cap for the Service that is pre‑approved, transparent, and periodically reviewed
   with stakeholder input.
17. Ensure Pricing Reflects Emergency‑Driven, Limited Use
    Compensation for the Service should reflect its emergency, infrequently deployed

    1. Of the two options described in the attached slides, an as-needed service or a seasonal

        It is our understanding that this Service is intended to provide a reliable, pre-identified

resource capable of delivering material reliability benefits to the electric grid in advance of
anticipated extreme weather events. Consistent with prior Commission direction and ERCOT

reliability programs, resources participating in this Service would be compensated in exchange

for making capacity available to support system reliability when conditions warrant.

       Given the anticipatory nature of the Service, we recommend that Commission Staff, the

Commission, and ERCOT establish clear, standardized protocols that allow resources to register

and qualify in advance of an anticipated event. A pre-registration framework would help ensure

that participating resources have demonstrated their ability to perform when called and would
provide ERCOT with greater confidence rega rding the magnitude and availability of committed

capacity.

       While ERCOT may often have advance notice of severe weather, there will inevitably be

circumstances in which changing forecasts or localized weather conditions create rapidly
escalating reliability concerns. In those instances, the Commission should avoid an approach that

relies on last-minute identification of eligible resources or ad hoc determinations of potential
curtailment capability. Such an approach increases operational uncertainty and undermines the

reliability value the Service is intended to provide.


                                                  2
        A standardized and pre-planned structure would align with existing ERCOT protocols

governing other reliability services, including the use of advance qualification, defined
operational parameters, and clear performance obligations. This approach would also provide

large load customers operating complex facilities with the predictability needed to incorporate
participation into their operational planning. A repeatable and well-defined process allows

participants to execute curtailment obligations consistently and effectively as extreme weather
events unfold, ratherthan reacting in real time under uncertain conditions.

       Accordingly, we recommend that the Commission direct ERCOT to implement this Service

through an advance qualification and registration framework, consistent with existing ERCOT

reliability service constructs, under which participating resources are identified, validated, and
enrolled ahead of anticipated extreme weather events. This framework should include clearly

defined operational requirements, notification timelines, and performance expectations. Doing

so will ensure that the Service delivers predictable and dependable reliability value, remains

administratively manageable for ERCOT, and provides participating resources with the certainty

necessary to commit capacity in a manner fully aligned with prior PUCT orders and ERCOT

protocols.

    2.   Deferred or delayed transmission or substation infrastructure.

       In developing these protocols, additional clarification is needed rega rding the distinction

between an "as-needed" and a "seasonal" Service. Under our understanding, an "as-needed"

construct would imply that the Service exists, but eligible large load participants are identified

                                                6
 and enrolled only immediately prior to an anticipated extreme weather or emergency condition.
By contrast, a "seasonal" construct would involve identifying, qualifying, and enrolling

participating resources in advance, with large loads having clear notice that they may be called
upon during a defined time period.

        We believe that a "seasonal" approach is more workable and better aligned with the

operational realities of large load facilities, including data centers. Advance enrollment allows

operators to conduct periodic testing, confirm willingness to participate, and validate operational
capabilities prior to an event. It also enables participants to clearly define ramp rates, test internal

systems, and ensure that onsite equipment and procedures can perform as required when the
Service is activated. This advance preparation is particularly important where partial curtailment,

rather than full shutdown, is expected.

        Depending on system needs, a large load exceeding 75 MW may be asked to curtail all or

only a portion of its load. For example, a 400 MW data center may be requested to curtail 100

MW within a 24-hour time frame. The actual time needed to achieve that reduction can vary

significantly depending on the facility's electrical configuration, applicable Service Level

Agreements, and installed onsite equipment. In some cases, load reductionscan be implemented

within minutes; in others, shifting or curtailing a portion of load may require additional
coordination, sequencing, and operational adjustments to maintain reliability within the facility.

        For this reason, we encourage that the guidelines and deployment protocols clearly

identify which resources will be called during curtailment events, the expected magnitude of
curtailment, and the applicable notification and performance timelines. While full curtailment of

an entire facility may be achieved quickly in certain configurations, partial curtailment scenarios
often require more deliberate operational steps and cannot be executed instantaneously without
prior planning. Establishing clear, advance expectations will allow participating large load

customersto respond efficientlyand reliably, while ensuringthat ERCOT receives dependable and

timely reliability support when system conditions warrant.

        b. What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39. I 70(b), if any, should apply
           to participation in the new service?
                                                   1
        PURA §39.170 establishes a targeted reliability service intended to support ERCOT's ability

to manage grid conditions during extreme weatherevents, while setting forth specific and limited
eligibility restrictions. The statute expressly prohibits participation only where a large load

customer curtails in response to wholesale electricity prices determined by ERCOT or otherwise

participates in a different reliabilityor ancillary service. Beyond these enumerated limitations, the

Legislature did not impose additional prohibitions on eligibility. Notably, the statute does not

restrict participation by large load customers that operate under Commission-approved

net-metering arrangements, nor does it exclude loads colocated with generation. Under

well-established principles of statutory interpretation, eligibility exclusions should be confined to
those expressly identified by the Legislature and should not be expanded through implication or

administrative interpretation.

       A Commission-approved net-metering arrangement does not, by itself, constitute

participation in an ERCOT market product, reliability service, or ancillary service. Net metering

governs the measurement and settlement of energy flows between a load and colocated
generation; it does not establish performance obligations, price exposure, or compensation
mechanisms comparable to ERCOT reliability or ancillary services. Treating net-metered entities

as ineligible would improperly conflate metering and settlement structures with market
participation. A large load with onsite or colocated generation remains an end-use customer

capable of providing load curtailment and operational flexibility. Eligibility forthe Service should

therefore be assessed based on operational behavior and performance capability, ratherthan the
presence of a net-metering configuration.

       Allowing participation by colocated large loads can meaningfully enhance grid reliability

and is fullyconsistent with the objectives of PURA §39.170. In many cases, a large load co-located

next to a generation resource may receive all or a portion of its normal operating power from that
facility. During grid emergencies, the generator may reduce service to the colocated load and

export power to the ERCOT grid, increasing system supply. At the same time, the large load may

curtail part or all of its demand, operate onsite emergency generation, or dispatch battery energy
storage resources to further reduce net load. These actions provide reliability benefits that are


                                                  8
 equivalent to, and in some cases exceed, traditional curtailment mechanisms, particularly when
they can be executed pursuant to pre-planned operational              protocols.   Excluding such

arrangements would unnecessarily eliminate resources that are capable of delivering reliable,
measurable, and controllable support during periods of system stress.

        Exclusion of net-metered, colocated large loads would also conflict with the Legislature's

intent in enacting SB 6. SB 6 explicitly encouraged large load customers to pursue net-metered

and colocated arrangements with generation as a means to accelerate economic development,
reduce pressure on the transmission system, and improve overall grid reliability. Interpreting

PURA §39.170 toprohibit participation bythose samearrangements would underminethat policy

objective and create a disincentive for investments the Legislature sought to promote. Nothing in

the statutory framework suggests an intent to penalize large load customers that have invested
in facilities designed to align with reliability goals.

        Accordingly, CyrusOne respectfully submits that no additional prohibitions beyond those

expressly stated in PURA §39.170(b) should apply to participation in the Service. Net-metered

large load customers approved under SB 6 should remain eligible, provided they do not engage

in price-responsive curtailment or participate in overlapping ERCOT reliability or ancillary

services. Eligibility determinations should focus on operational conduct and performance, not

metering structure. Allowing participation by net-metered, colocated large loads will broaden the

pool of reliable resources available to ERCOT, enhance system resilience, and further the

Legislature's dual objectives of maintaining grid reliability and supporting continued economic

development in Texas..


        c. Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such as four
            coincident peak (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude participation in the new
            service?
        From the standpoint of a data center operator, participation in price responsiveness aimed

at managing transmission-related cost exposure-such as the Four Coincident Peak ("4CP")

methodology or any successor approach-should not, standing alone, disqualify a load from
participating in the new Service. These activities address different problems and operate on

different time horizons. Price responsiveness to transmission cost drivers is a routine,

                                                     9
 economically rational practice that helps customers manage long-term cost allocation and
informs planning outcomes. By contrast, the Service contemplated under PURA § 39.170(b) is a

narrowly tailored reliability tool, intended for infrequent deployment during extreme weather
driven by emergency conditions and likely subject to specific notice, duration, and performance
requirements.
       A blanket prohibition based on 4CP participation would likely exclude exactly the types of

large, operationally sophisticated loads that are best positioned to provide dependable,
measurable curtailment at the scale envisioned by the statute. Such an outcome would weaken

the effectiveness of the service without advancing reliability objectives. The more appropriate

regulatory concern is not whether a participant engages in price-responsive behavior in other
contexts, but whetherthe same load reduction is being counted orcompensated twice. That issue

can be addressed through clear eligibility criteria, disclosure requirements, and post-event
verification to ensure that curtailments provided under the new service are incremental,
reliability-driven, and distinct from routine cost-management actions, while still allowing large
loads to engage responsibly in both frameworks.

We do not have a current position on how it should be defined, but reserve the right to provide

   4. How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new service?

       This Service should be structured and deployed as a credible, last-resort reliability

backstop intended for use during extreme weather conditions, rather than as a standing capacity
product or an economic demand response mechanism. Its purpose should be narrowly tailored

to support ERCOT's ability to manage acute system reliability risks, and it should function as a

complement to-rather than a replacement for-existing tools such as emergency reserves,
emergency imports, and ERCOT's established EEA framework. Preserving this distinction is

essentialto maintainingthe Service's emergencycharacterand ensuring it is leveraged only when

system conditions warrant.

                                               10
        To that end, a reasonable target quantity for the Service would be on the order of 1-5

percent of ERCOT's forecasted peak load for applicable extreme weather seasons, with the target

recalculated annually to reflect changing system conditions and load growth. Establishing a

defined MW target provides predictability for participating resources and gives ERCOT confidence

that a known quantity of committed and callable capacity will be available during critical periods,
without creating incentives for over-procurement or routine use.

       From a budget and pricing perspective, we encourage the Commission and ERCOT to

adopt a clearly defined annual or seasonal budget cap for the Service that is pre-approved,

transparent, and subject to periodic review with sta keholder input. Budget sizing should be

informed by the targeted MW quantity and the maximum anticipated duration of deployment

under emergency conditions. A defined          budget framework protects against excessive

procurement, provides participating large loads with clarity that compensation reflects the true
emergency value of the Service, and supports ERCOT's operational planning objectives. Given the

Service's intended role as an infrequently deployed reliability backstop, pricing should

appropriately reflect its limited and emergency-driven use, rather than incentivizing routine
dispatch or participation for economic reasons.

   5. What additional information should the Commission consider in its implementation of
       PURA§ 39.170(b)?

       In implementing PURA §39.170(b), it would be beneficial for the Commission to provide

clarity rega rding how the Service is intended to function in circumstances involving localized or

targeted reliability constraints, rather than solely system-wide emergency conditions. While

ERCOT's Energy Emergency Alert (EEA) framework appropriately addresses broader system

reliability issues, experience has shown that extreme weather events often interact with localized
infrastructure limitations in ways that can create acute reliability risks absent a system-wide
emergency declaration. Examples include load pockets with limited import capability, delayed or

deferred substation or transformer upgrades, or the outage of a single large transmission
element, such as a 345-kV line. Under normal conditions, these constraints may be manageable;




                                                  11
 however, when compounded by localized extreme weather, they may result in localized
emergency conditions that warrant targeted reliability interventions.

       As the Commission considers how the Service may be deployed to address these localized

risks, it is also important to consider the practical characteristics of the resources that would be
expected to respond, particularly large loads with backup generation assets. Many large load

facilities, including data centers, maintain onsite diesel generation fleets designed first and
foremost for reliability and safety, not continuous operation. These fleets may include a

combination of Tier 2 and Tier 4 engines, each governed by different air emissions standards and

operating limitations. Participation in the Service may require these resources to operate outside

traditional assumptions for backup generator usage, particularly if activation occurs in
anticipation of extreme weather rather than during a clearly defined emergency.

       From an air permitting perspective, it is not yet clear whether operation under this Service

would qualify as "emergency" operation for purposes of federal or state air emissions
requirements. If Service deployment occurs preemptively-prior to an EEA declaration or prior to

conditions meeting traditional emergency definitions-runtime associated with participation
may not clearly fall within existing emergency exemptions under Clean Air Act permitting

frameworks. This distinction has material implications for large load participants, as generators

may require updated permits or permit modifications to lawfully support participation in the
Service.


       Accordingly, we believe it is critical for the Commission to coordinate closely with the

Texas Commission on Environmental Quality ("TCEQ") and, where appropriate, the U.S.

Environmental Protection Agency ("EPA"), to ensure that expectations for generator operation

under the Service are clearly understood and consistently applied. Participants need clarity

regarding the range of potential operating scenarios that may be expected under the Service,

includinganticipatedduration, frequency, and notice periods forgeneratoroperation. Suchclarity

is essential to determine whether additional permitting is required and to avoid creating
regulatory uncertainty that could discourage participation.



                                                 12
        As part of this coordination, it would be helpful forthe Commission and TCEQ to consider

whether enforcement discretion or other compliance assurances may be appropriate in narrowly
defined circumstances where generator operation is undertaken in good-faith compliance with
the Service to support grid reliability, particularly where deviations from permit conditions are

limited in duration and not indicative of routine or prolonged non-compliance. While we

recognize that air quality protections remain paramount, clear guidance on how agencies intend
to treat generator operation undertaken at ERCOT's direction or in coordination with

Commission-approved      reliability   programs   would     meaningfully   reduce    uncertainty for

participants.

       Ultimately, thoughtful alignment between the PUCT, ERCOT, TCEQ, and EPA will be

essential to the successful      implementation        of PURA §39.170(b).      Providing clarity on

environmental compliance expectations will enable large loads with backup generation to assess
participation realistically, ensure adherence to applicable emissions requirements, and support
the Service's reliability objectives without unintended regulatory conflicts.

     compensated.
12. Establish Clear Qualification Criteria for Load Ramp-Down Timeframes

     The Commission and ERCOT should define qualification standards that recognize some


                                              16
    large loads may require up to 24 hours to safely achieve full or partial curtailment,
   depending on configuration, SLAs, and onsite equipment.

13. Define Clear Notification, Performance, and Magnitude Expectations

    Deployment protocols should clearly identify which resources will be called, the amount

   of curtailment expected, and applicable notification and performance timelines to
   enable reliable and orderly execution.
14. Structure the Service as a Last-Resort Reliability Backstop

    The Service should be explicitly designed as an infrequently used, last-resort reliability

   tool for extreme weather conditions, not as a standing capacity product or economic
   demand response mechanism.
15. Set a Reasonable MW Target Based on Seasonal Peak Load

    The Commission should establish a target quantity for the Service of approximately 1-5

   percent of ERCOT's forecasted peak load during extreme weather seasons and

   recalculate the target annually.
16. Adopt a Transparent, Pre-Approved Budget Cap

    The Commission and ERCOT should establish a clearly defined annual or seasonal

   budget cap for the Service that is pre-approved, transparent, and periodically reviewed

   with stakeholder input.
17. Ensure Pricing Reflects Emergency-Driven, Limited Use

    Compensation for the Service should reflect its emergency, infrequently deployed

   nature and should not incentivize routine dispatch or price-driven participation.
18. Coordinate with TCEQ and EPA on Air Permitting for Backup Generation

    The Commission should coordinate with the Texas Commission on Environmental

   Quality and the U.S. EPA to clarify how generator operation under the Service will be

   treated under air permitting rules, particularly where activation may not qualify as
   "emergency" operation.
19. Clarify Permitting Expectations and Potential Enforcement Discretion

    The Commission should work with environmental regulators to provide clarity on

   whether enforcement discretion or compliance assurances may apply where generators


                                            17
    operate in good-faith compliance with the Service for short durations to support grid

   reliability.
20. Include Direction Implementing PURA §39.170(a) Where Appropriate

   The Commission should address the requirements of PURA §39.170(a) in this

   rulemaking to ensure coordinated implementation with the Service under subsection

   (b), while avoiding duplicative or prescriptive requirements already addressed through
   ERCOT protocols.
